newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian Treasury rings in telecom changes.
newsitem.headline: Italian Treasury rings in telecom changes.

text.p: The Italian Treasury said on Friday it would replace the top two executives at telecommunications holding Stet as it prepares the company for privatisation later this year.
The Treasury also said that the conglomerate would absorb the telephone operating firm Telecom Italia as part of a plan to streamline management within the group.

Full terms of the fusion are expected to be completed between the end of June and the end of August with the much-delayed privatisation of one of the world's largest telecommunications groups now scheduled by the end of October.
The Treasury, which took command of Stet at the start of the year, announced that Stet's managing director Ernesto Pascale and company chairman Biagio Agnes had agreed to step down.
Pascale, who said earlier this month that he only expected to leave Stet once it had been sold, will be replaced by Tommasi di Vignano, who is currently director-general of Telecom Italia.
Agnes's position will be filled by Guido Rossi, the former head of the Italian bourse regulator Consob who led Italian industrial giant Ferruzzi out of financial crisis in the mid-1990s.
"The Treasury, Industry and Telecommunications Ministries wish to express their deep appreciation for the work carried out by Agnes and Pascale," the Treasury statement said.
The move to oust the two men is bound to cause controversy in a highly politicised sector, with 62-year old Pascale firmly backed by the centre-right opposition.
"We have now broken all limits," said Maurizio Gasparri, a senior official within the hard right National Alliance party.

The Treasury has taken little time to ring in the changes at Stet since taking over control of the company from state holding IRI and is committed to privatising the telecoms sector before the end of 1997.
The state holds just over 60 percent of Stet, which in turn holds 63.4 percent of Telecom Italia.

The two firms are due to hold board meetings on January 30 to give the official go-ahead for the fusion which will create a group which had a combined turnover of some 40 trillion lire ($25.2 billion) in 1996.
The company, which will keep the name Telecom Italia, will continue to control separately listed cellular phone group Telecom Italia Mobile along with a number of cable and engineering firms.

Italians have dubbed the planned sale of Stet as the "mother of all privatisations," but the flotation has been regularly postponed in the past and political bickering continues to cast a shadow over the planned sell-off.

Legislation needed for the sale is still blocked in parliament and a key government ally, the hardleft Communist Refoundation, has threatened to bring down Prime Minister Romano Prodi's coalition if it presses ahead with the privatisation.
Government officials in recent days have held behind-the- scenes meetings with Refoundation, which is ideologically opposed to the sell-off, to try to break the deadlock over Stet.
"Italy is risking its credibility with the privatisations over the coming months," Giorgio Fossa, the head of employers' federation Confindustria, warned on Friday.
